# Viruses and the host

> *Influenza virus makes a person ill for about a week and is then cleared, whereas HIV stays for
> life and causes disease years after infection. The difference lies in which cells each virus can
> infect, how the host responds to the infection, and whether the virus can persist.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Relate the cells a virus infects to the receptors it binds, using influenza virus and HIV.
- Distinguish a local infection at the site of entry from systemic spread through lymph, blood or
  nerves.
- Describe four patterns of viral damage, and give an anchor example of each.
- Explain how the loss of CD4 T cells in HIV infection allows opportunistic infections.
- Distinguish acute, latent and chronic viral infection, and relate each to when damage occurs.
:::

## Entry and spread {#sec-vhost-entry}

### Receptors and tropism {#sec-vhost-receptors}

A virus begins its replication cycle by attaching to a molecule on the surface of a host cell, its
**receptor** (see [*How viruses are built and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-cycle)).
Only cells that carry the receptor can be infected, so the distribution of the receptor sets the
virus's tropism, the range of cells and tissues it can occupy (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-steps)). Tropism in turn decides which organ is
damaged.

::: {.example}
Influenza virus attaches by its haemagglutinin (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-envelope)) to sialic acid, a sugar on the
epithelial cells lining the airway, so it infects the airway and the alveoli.
:::

Some viruses need two molecules on the cell surface. HIV attaches first to **CD4**, a protein on the
surface of **CD4 T cells** (helper T cells), the lymphocytes that coordinate the immune response,
including the activity of macrophages and of the T cells that kill infected cells. It then binds a
second molecule, a **co-receptor**, before its envelope fuses with the cell membrane.

::: {.example}
CD4 and a co-receptor are found together on CD4 T cells and macrophages, so these are the cells HIV
infects, and the immune system is what it damages.
:::

### Local and systemic infection {#sec-vhost-spread}

A virus enters at a body surface: the airway, the gut, the genital tract, or the skin, through a
bite or a needle. Some viruses stay at the site of entry and cause a local infection. Others spread
through the body and cause a systemic infection. **Viraemia** is the presence of virus in the blood,
and it carries a virus to organs far from where it entered.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Where a virus goes after entry]{.tree-title}

- After entry at a body surface
  - Stays local: infects the epithelium at the site of entry, as influenza virus does in the airway
  - Spreads beyond the site of entry
    - In lymph: to the regional lymph nodes, where lymphocytes and macrophages gather
    - In blood (viraemia): free in the plasma or inside infected white blood cells, to organs
      throughout the body
    - In nerves: along the axon to the nerve cell body ([latent infection](#sec-vhost-latency))
:::

::: {.example}
New influenza virus buds from the surface of the epithelial cell that faces the airway lumen, so it
is released into the airway, where it infects neighbouring cells and is breathed out to the next
host; it rarely enters the blood.
:::

A local infection does not have to spread through the body first, so its incubation period (see
[*Transmission, outbreaks and One Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-measures))
is short: a few days for influenza.

::: {.example}
HIV that enters through the genital or rectal mucosa infects CD4 T cells and macrophages there, is
carried in lymph to the regional lymph nodes, which are full of CD4 T cells, and then reaches the
blood, which carries it to lymphoid tissue throughout the body.
:::

A virus that circulates in the blood can also be transmitted by blood, through shared needles or
transfusion (see [*Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses*](bloodborne-viruses.qmd)).

## Patterns of damage {#sec-vhost-damage}

Viruses damage the host in four ways, and a single infection often combines more than one.

| Pattern | Mechanism | Anchor example |
|---|---|---|
| Death of infected cells | The virus takes over the cell's machinery, and the cell dies | Influenza virus killing the ciliated epithelium of the airway |
| Damage by the immune response | Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells; inflammation damages the tissue around them | Inflammation in the airway and alveoli in severe influenza |
| Loss of the cells the virus infects | The infected cells have a function the body needs, and their loss leaves a gap in it | HIV depleting CD4 T cells, so that cell-mediated immunity fails |
| Transformation to cancer | Viral proteins override the cell's controls on division | Human papillomavirus and cancer of the cervix |

On the damage-response framework (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)), death of infected cells and transformation
are damage done by the virus, and immune-mediated damage is done by the host's response. Most viral
diseases involve both.

### Death of infected cells {#sec-vhost-cpe}

An infected cell makes viral proteins and genomes with its own ribosomes, energy and building
blocks, and many viruses shut down the cell's own protein synthesis. The damage that results, often
ending in the death of the cell, is the **cytopathic effect**. The same changes can be seen when a
virus is grown in cells in the laboratory (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-methods)). Viruses that leave the cell by budding (see [*How
viruses are built and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-cycle)) can release
new particles for some time before the cell dies, whereas many non-enveloped viruses are released
when the cell bursts.

::: {.example}
Influenza virus kills the ciliated epithelial cells of the trachea and bronchi, and the damaged lining
clears mucus and bacteria poorly, so a bacterial pneumonia, for example with *Staphylococcus aureus*,
can follow.
:::

### The host response {#sec-vhost-immune}

The first defence against a virus begins within the infected tissue. An infected cell releases
**interferon**, a signal that puts neighbouring cells into an antiviral state in which they resist
infection. Interferon and other signals released early in infection also contribute to the fever and
aching of an acute viral illness.

Later, the adaptive immune response clears the virus. **Cytotoxic T cells** recognise viral proteins
displayed on the surface of an infected cell and kill that cell. Killing the cell removes a source of
new virus, but the dead cells are the host's own. Antibodies bind virus particles outside cells and
block their attachment to new ones. Inflammation recruits these cells and fluid to the site, and, as
in general pathology, inflammation that clears an infection also damages the tissue in which it
occurs.

::: {.example}
In severe influenza, inflammation extends from the airway into the alveoli, and fluid and
inflammatory cells in the alveoli impair gas exchange.
:::

Where much of the damage comes from the response, a stronger response can mean more disease, as on
the right-hand side of the damage-response curves.

### Loss of the cells the virus infects {#sec-vhost-cd4}

When the cells a virus infects have a function the body cannot do without, their loss causes
disease far from the site of infection. HIV kills CD4 T cells, both directly and through cytotoxic T
cells that recognise infected cells, and over years their number falls.

::: {.flow}
1. HIV infects CD4 T cells
2. Infected cells are killed
3. CD4 T-cell count falls over years
4. Cell-mediated immunity fails
5. Opportunistic infections
:::

Without CD4 T cells, cell-mediated immunity fails: the defence against organisms that live inside
host cells (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)).
Organisms that a person with intact defences controls can then cause disease, as opportunistic
infections. This advanced stage of HIV infection is the **acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
(AIDS)**.

::: {.example}
Tuberculosis is a common opportunistic infection in advanced HIV infection, because the control of
*Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, which survives inside macrophages, depends on cell-mediated immunity.
:::

### Viruses and cancer {#sec-vhost-cancer}

A few viruses can change an infected cell so that it divides without normal control, and over years
such cells can give rise to a cancer. A virus that can cause cancer is an **oncogenic virus**. The
change in the cell is called transformation, a word that means something different in bacteria,
where it is the uptake of free DNA (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](../bacteria/bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-hgt)). Cancer follows in only a small proportion
of infected people, and only after years, because further changes in the cell are needed.

::: {.example}
Human papillomavirus causes almost all cancers of the cervix. Two of its proteins inactivate the
cell's tumour-suppressor proteins, which normally halt the division of a cell with damaged DNA, and
infection that persists for years can lead to cancer.
:::

## Persistence {#sec-vhost-persistence}

Viral infections follow the acute, latent and chronic time courses (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-courses)). For viruses these are points on a range,
set by how much virus is produced after the first illness.

::: {.spectrum}
[Virus produced after the first illness]{.tree-title}

- Acute, influenza virus: cleared within days to weeks
- Latent, herpesviruses: the genome stays silent in cells for life, and virus is produced only when
  it reactivates
- Chronic, HIV: virus produced continuously for years

[None]{.spectrum-end} [Continuous]{.spectrum-end}
:::

### Acute infection {#sec-vhost-acute}

In an acute infection the virus multiplies rapidly, is transmitted, and is cleared by the immune
response within days to weeks. Influenza virus is the anchor. Immunity to that strain remains after
recovery, although the virus changes enough to infect the same person again in later years (see
[*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-consequences)). Damage comes early and from both
sources: the cytopathic effect in the airway epithelium and the inflammation that clears it.

### Latent infection {#sec-vhost-latency}

In a latent infection the viral genome stays in a cell without producing new virus. The cell makes
few or no viral proteins, so cytotoxic T cells cannot recognise it. From time to time the virus
reactivates, produces new virus, and can cause disease and be transmitted again. Little damage occurs
between reactivations.

::: {.example}
Herpes simplex virus, the common example of latency in nerve cells, travels along sensory nerves
from the skin or mucosa to the nerve cell bodies, persists there for life, and can return along the
nerve to cause recurrent lesions at the same site (see [*Herpesviruses*](herpesviruses.qmd)).
:::

Reactivation is more frequent and more damaging when cell-mediated immunity falls, as in advanced HIV
infection. The same principle explains why HIV is never cleared: its provirus (see [*How viruses are
built and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)) persists in
long-lived resting CD4 T cells that make no virus, out of reach of the immune response.

### Chronic infection {#sec-vhost-chronic}

In a chronic infection the virus continues to replicate for months or years despite an immune
response. HIV is the anchor: virus is produced continuously, the CD4 T-cell count falls slowly, and
disease appears years after infection. Damage accumulates over that time as CD4 T cells are lost, and
the infected person can transmit the virus throughout, often without knowing of the infection.
